source.title: PROST: Physical Reasoning about Objects through Space and Time
source.authors: Stephane T Aroca-Ouellette; Cory Paik; Alessandro Roncone; Katharina Kann

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-related downstream performance using PROST accuracy rather than held-out cross-entropy loss, and reports whether accuracy changes across model sizes.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure pretraining loss, fit power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its own scale-related results are PROST accuracy comparisons. Results about answer order and superlative inverses do not measure the listed scaling versions. The PIQA fine-tuning result is recorded separately because it concerns a training regime rather than scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The study compares zero-shot PROST accuracy across sizes within GPT-2, BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT V2, T5 and UnifiedQA (Table 5, Fig. 2). That is a direct result on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6), in a new setting: physical-reasoning probes. It explicitly contrasts its findings with Kaplan et al. It does not measure pretraining loss, fit curves or vary allocation, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that larger parameter counts and more pretraining data give only minimal PROST improvements, with exceptions where larger models do worse. They conclude scaling text-only models is unlikely to solve physical reasoning and that grounded, multimodal experience is needed.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a zero-shot multiple-choice physical-reasoning benchmark and accuracy, not held-out language-model loss, fitted scaling laws, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: PROST accuracy varies by concept, model family and size; the paper also reports sensitivity to answer order and superlative inversion, though those analyses do not test the listed scaling versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Further PIQA finetuning of UnifiedQA 3B lowers PROST macro accuracy: 45.31% at the best-PIQA checkpoint vs 47.44% at the best-PROST checkpoint (Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finetuning on a related physical-reasoning dataset can reduce zero-shot performance on a differently formatted physical-reasoning probe.

record.problems: The study reports accuracy rather than pretraining loss and does not fit scaling curves or isolate scale from model family, architecture, training data, and fine-tuning. It provides no uncertainty estimates. T5 and UnifiedQA averages omit sliding, and the paper does not report a direct human accuracy comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scale-related aggregate rows were left out. Non-scaling analyses of answer-option position, superlative inverses, and individual PROST concepts were omitted except for the T5 bounceable comparison, because they do not test V6's scale-or-loss predictability statement.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss; any fitted trend or predictive form; scale isolated from model family and data (the data-scaling axis in Fig. 2 is confounded across families).
Not tested: no fits or extrapolation.
Not tested: no controlled shape comparison.
Not tested: no loss power laws in other regimes.
Not tested: no exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: GPT-2 size series macro accuracy: B 23.6%, M 26.8%, L 26.4%, XL 30.1%. Only M vs L is recorded, and that as prose without values; B and XL rows are absent.
missing.locator: Table 5, GPT-2 rows, Macro Average column

missing.what: Accuracy vs amount of pretraining data across families (2–170 GB), with circle size showing parameters; the authors read it as little improvement.
missing.locator: Figure 2; Section 6 Data and Model Scaling

record.verdict_notes: Scale comparisons are within model families but uncontrolled across families (different data and objectives). There are no uncertainty estimates. T5 and UnifiedQA averages exclude the sliding concept. UnifiedQA's large gains coincide with QA finetuning, so they are not pure pretraining scale.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions; several-orders-of-magnitude power-law behavior.
No power-law fits on small runs or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation comparison or parameter/token optima.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of scaling-law forms in other modalities or of power laws under repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance analysis; the paper measures PROST accuracy across model sizes, not downstream performance across a broad task suite.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal split are compared across counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Pretrained-only families (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT V2 B to XL, T5) on PROST macro accuracy
relationships.reason: Larger models score higher but only by 1–6 points near 25% chance; T5-3B gains 6.6 points for 48x parameters (r2-r5, r6-r8, r10-r13).
relationships.display_finding: Larger models generally gain only 1–6 points near the 25% chance level, with T5-3B gaining 6.6 points for 48-fold more parameters.

relationships.reason: Macro accuracy rises from 26.6% (S) to 39.2% (L) and 46.7% (3B), though S to B shows no gain (r16-r19).
relationships.display_finding: Macro accuracy increased from 26.6% for S to 39.2% for L and 46.7% for 3B, despite no improvement from S to B.

relationships.condition: ALBERT V2 XL to XXL, GPT-2 M to L, T5 bounceable concept
relationships.reason: Larger models score lower: ALBERT XXL 29.8% vs XL 31.8%, GPT-2 L 26.4% vs M 26.8%, T5-3B bounceable 12.5% vs small 30.2% (r8-r9, r20, r14-r15).
relationships.display_finding: ALBERT XXL scored 29.8% versus XL's 31.8%, GPT-2 L scored 26.4% versus M's 26.8%, and T5-3B scored 12.5% on bounceable versus small's 30.2%.
